pilotr includes a point-and-click application over the same design specification that the R
and Python packages read. Every control in the app writes into the portable JSON specification.

## Two ways to run it

One way is to run it on your own machine. The app needs the shiny and ggplot2 packages, which
pilotr suggests but does not install, so install them first and then launch the app locally:

```{r}
install.packages(c("shiny", "ggplot2"))
pilotr::run_app()
```

Each user runs their own R process, so a power run never holds up anyone else. Within the app,
each power analysis or power curve runs in one R process, and the app waits for its result. With
the future and promises packages installed, `run_app()` runs it in a background process, leaving
the app free for other sessions, such as a second browser tab. For a heavy run, download the
specification and call `power_design()` or `power_mixed()` from the console. Their `workers`
argument spreads the replicates over your local cores.

The installed app caps the simulations of a power analysis, and of each point of a power curve,
at 5,000. To change the cap, set the `PILOTR_MAX_SIMS` environment variable before calling
`run_app()`, for example with `Sys.setenv(PILOTR_MAX_SIMS = 20000)`.

The other way needs nothing installed. A serverless build runs entirely in the browser
through WebAssembly, and nothing is uploaded. Try it at the
[no-code app](https://pablobernabeu.github.io/pilotr/app/). It covers the lighter tasks:
building a design, simulating, inspecting the data, estimating two-group Gaussian power with
the sample size its curve solves to, and exporting.

## What the app does

Describe the design in the left panel: the sample sizes, the factor and its two levels, the
fixed intercept and effect, a response family, and for crossed designs the random-effect
standard deviations. Changing the response family resets the intercept and effect to sensible
values for that family's scale. A within design crossed with items can use counterbalanced
lists, which show each subject each item in one condition and rotate the conditions over
subjects and items. A specification that uses counterbalanced lists declares version 0.4. The
advanced 'paste a JSON spec' box accepts designs beyond the point-and-click controls, such as
continuous predictors, interactions and nesting.

Then read the tabs. Both apps open on 'Guide', which describes the controls, the response
families and the analyses. Three of the other tabs have shorter names in the browser build,
given here in brackets after the installed app's. 'Design spec (JSON)' ('Design spec') holds the
exact JSON specification, and 'Data' the simulated data set. 'Summary & plot' gives group
summaries and a plot.

'Power & design analysis' ('Power') runs a power analysis for a two-group Gaussian design with
one row per subject, and for any other design it explains how to run one in the installed
package. For a two-group Gaussian design, it reports simulation-based power with the Type S and
Type M errors. It also gives a power curve over sample size and the sample size at which that
curve reaches 0.80, with a confidence interval on it. The curve adds sample sizes until it
brackets a power of 0.80. For a design without random effects or continuous predictors, the tab
also gives the sample size `power.t.test()` computes, as a check.

'Reproducible R script' ('R script') emits a self-contained R script that reproduces the data
and ends by suggesting the analysis that fits the design. In the installed app, 'Verify' runs
that script in a clean R session and checks that its data are identical, bit for bit, to the
data the current specification produces. The comparison is with the specification in force when
you select 'Verify', so it does not depend on when you last selected 'Simulate'. 'Verify' needs
the callr package.

'Data', 'Summary & plot' and the data download show the last simulation, and the 'Data' tab and
the name of the downloaded file give the seed it used. The specification, power and script tabs
and the specification download follow the controls as they stand. When the controls change the
design after a simulation, a note above the tabs says so until you select 'Simulate' again.

## One specification, three interfaces

From the app, you can download the specification (`.json`) or the data (`.csv`). The
specification runs unchanged in R with `simulate_design()` or in Python with `pilotr.simulate()`
for the same data, identical to the last bit wherever R and Python share a maths library (see the
[cross-language article](cross-language.html)). The app rounds Gaussian and reaction-time
responses to four decimals and leaves a Beta response unrounded, for the reason `?build_spec`
gives.

The app leaves the heavier analyses to the installed packages. Crossed mixed-effects power runs
in R, through `lme4` as the reference backend, and in Python, through `statsmodels`.
Precision/ROPE design analysis runs in R.
